segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We came in sight of Cyprus and, leaving it on our left, sailed on to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When our days there were up, we left and went on our way, and all of them, with wives and children, escorted us until we were outside the city. Kneeling on the beach, we prayed

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said farewell to one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they returned home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais, and after greeting the brothers and sisters we stayed with them one day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While we were staying there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and hand him over into the hands of Gentiles.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we heard this, we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since he would not be persuaded, we fell silent, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Lord’s will be done.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these days we got ready and started up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us, bringing us to the man with whom we were to lodge, Mnason, a Cypriot and a disciple from the early days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters welcomed us gladly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After greeting them, he recounted one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his service.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard it, they glorified God, and they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: They have been told about you that you teach all the Jews living among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or live by the customs.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow on themselves.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Take them, be purified with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also keep in step, observing the law.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent word of our decision that they should keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul took the men, and the next day, having been purified with them, he went into the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, when the offering would be made for each one of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. What is more, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The whole city was roused, and the people came running together. They took hold of Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were trying to kill him, a report went up to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the tribune came up, took hold of him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains; and he began asking who he was and what he had done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. Since he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the mass of the people was following, shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Away with him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was about to be brought into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May I say something to you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You know Greek?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Then you are not the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had given permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand to the people. When a great silence had fallen, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address or describe a mixed group of men and women, and here it refers to the whole local community of believers. ‘Brothers’ alone now suggests men only. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep ‘brothers’ as the more literal form.

The Seven are the men appointed in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food (Acts 6:1–6). The description distinguishes this Philip, who had preached in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (Acts 8), from Philip the apostle.

The word denotes a young woman who has not married, with virginity assumed and not separately asserted. The point here is the daughters’ status in their father’s household, so ‘unmarried’ conveys what a first-century reader would have taken from it. Some interpreters think a deliberate commitment to celibacy is implied, but the text does not say so.

One Greek word means both ‘a nation’ or ‘people’ and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples as a group. This translation uses ‘Gentiles’ for the second sense and ‘nation’ or ‘nations’ for the first; both render the same word.

notes.phrase: bringing us to the man with whom we were to lodge
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and can also be read as ‘bringing with them Mnason, with whom we were to lodge’. Most translations take it as rendered here. It is also unclear whether Mnason’s house was in Jerusalem or at a stopping place on the two-day journey from Caesarea.

The word means service rendered or a task carried out on someone’s behalf. ‘Ministry’ is the traditional rendering and is still used by most translations, but it now suggests a clerical profession or office, which the Greek word does not.

notes.phrase: They will certainly hear that you have come.
notes.traditional: the multitude must needs come together: for they will hear that thou art come
notes.note: Many later manuscripts have a longer reading: ‘a crowd must certainly gather, for they will hear that you have come.’ The shorter text translated here is found in several early witnesses and is the one printed in the SBLGNT.

The vow is generally understood to be a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which ended with shaving the head and offering several sacrifices at the temple. Paying for the offerings of Nazirites who could not afford them was regarded as an act of piety. How Paul’s own purification relates to the men’s vow is debated.

Non-Jews were allowed in the outer court of the temple, but a barrier marked off the inner courts, with notices warning that any foreigner who passed it would be liable to death. Josephus describes these notices, and inscribed examples have been found. The charge was therefore a capital one.

The Greek title, literally ‘commander of a thousand’, was the standard equivalent for a Roman military tribune. He commanded the cohort garrisoned in the Antonia fortress, which overlooked the temple courts and was connected to them by stairs. That is why the report ‘went up’ and the soldiers ‘ran down’. He is named in Acts 23:26 as Claudius Lysias.

The Greek borrows a Latin word for a man armed with a dagger, which was used for a murderer or assassin. Josephus applies it to Jewish militants of this period who stabbed their opponents in crowds. He also tells of an Egyptian prophet who led a large following to the Mount of Olives under the governor Felix and escaped when the Romans attacked. His figures for the Egyptian’s following differ from the number given here.

notes.traditional: in the Hebrew tongue; in Aramaic
notes.note: The Greek says literally ‘in the Hebrew dialect’. Many scholars take this to mean Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea, since Greek writers could call either language ‘Hebrew’. Others argue that Hebrew proper is meant. The question is unresolved, and the text is rendered literally.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural, of the community)
candidates.reason: The plural for the believing community recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translations split between ‘brothers’ and ‘brothers and sisters’; it needs one policy.
Recurs across Acts and Paul, where translators vary between ‘ministry’, ‘service’ and ‘mission’, and ‘ministry’ carries clerical overtones the Greek lacks.
Occurs repeatedly in Acts 21–25 and in the Gospels and Revelation, with translations varying between ‘tribune’, ‘commander’ and ‘captain’.
Occurs only here and names a specific faction; it may meet the loanword test (‘Sicarii’), since ‘assassins’ and ‘terrorists’ both carry misleading modern associations.

Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul and Revelation with renderings ranging from ‘fornication’ to ‘sexual immorality’ to ‘prostitution’, and consistency matters for the apostolic decree and the vice lists.
